history.content: Wound Rotor

A wound rotor, also known as a slip ring rotor or an induction rotor, is a type of rotor used in induction motors. It consists of a laminated iron core with multiple windings, typically three, wound on the core.

The windings are connected to external resistors or variable resistors through slip rings and brushes. These slip rings allow electrical connections to be made to the rotor windings, hence the name "slip ring rotor". The resistance in the rotor circuit can be adjusted to control certain characteristics of the motor, such as its speed and torque.

When the motor is started, the slip rings and brushes provide a low-resistance path for current to flow through the rotor windings. This allows a large starting torque to be generated, as the windings can draw a high current. As the motor speeds up, the resistance in the rotor circuit can be gradually reduced, allowing the motor to reach its maximum speed.

The wound rotor design offers several advantages over other types of rotors. It provides high starting torque, allows for adjustable speed control, and can handle higher loads without overheating. It is commonly used in applications where the motor needs to start under heavy load, such as in large pumps, compressors, and mills.

In summary, a wound rotor is a type of rotor used in induction motors that consists of multiple windings connected through slip rings. It provides high starting torque and allows for adjustable speed control.
